query: What are best-practice consent, signage, and opt-out protocols for dwell/zone sensor passive tracking that balance ethics with analytic linkage needs?

response.query: What are best-practice consent, signage, and opt-out protocols for dwell/zone sensor passive tracking that balance ethics with analytic linkage needs?
response.answer: Best-practice consent for passive tracking includes clear, informed opt-in, easy opt-out, and transparent data use. Signage should clearly indicate monitoring areas. Protocols must balance ethical considerations with analytic needs.

results.title: Paying for Privacy and the Personal Data Economy
results.content: 1372 COLUMBIA LAW REVIEW [Vol. 117:1369 Established data brokers have played a central role in the market for consumer data.7 A U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation staff report notes that data brokers compile information about consumers from various sources, including social media and con-tracts with other businesses.8 It is estimated that Acxiom, one of the largest data brokers, has approximately twenty-three thousand servers scrutinizing the data of millions of individuals.9 Once data brokers obtain consumer data, they frequently transfer this information to unaffiliated parties.10 The Internet of Things (IOT)—a network of connected devices— presents new opportunities for data brokers and other businesses to col-lect real-time and increasingly detailed data about the habits, lives, and activities of consumers.11 Companies that provide IOT consumer prod-ucts, such as Internet-enabled washing machines, thermostats, baby monitors, and security cameras, can use consumer data for their own purposes, and in many instances these companies may also transfer or disclose this information to third parties.12 These data include consump-tion-rate data, location data, health-related data, and recordings of children’s voices.13 Thus, what has “changed [in the data market] is the volume and nature of the data being mined from the Internet[,] .
